name: Lena Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a stroke rehabilitation ward, mostly on nights. People come to us after the acute bit, when they're relearning how to swallow, stand, talk. At night it's turning people every two hours, settling the confused ones, checking blood sugars, and a lot of quiet hand-holding at three in the morning. I like nights because it's calmer and nobody's rushing me. What wears me out is the sleep, and the computer at the end of the shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm not good with it. I still write my handover on paper first and then type it in, because the screen makes me freeze. Kofi, the senior nurse on nights, usually sorts my mistakes out before the morning team arrives. I know I need to get better, I just don't enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. That sounds about right to me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Every year there's a new thing that's going to change the NHS and it mostly ends up being a new password. I wouldn't post about it, I don't really post, but in the break room I'd shrug and say 'told you'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be glad. Less pressure to learn things I'm bad at. But night shifts on a stroke ward with rent going up every year is already the hard part, with or without AI. My one-bed flat went up sixty a month in the summer and I've only got about two months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep doing nights because they pay a bit more, keep trying to put fifty or so a month aside, and do the swallow assessment training my manager keeps nagging about. Maybe ask my parents for help with the deposit when my lease ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. Not about AI. About money, and whether I'm actually good enough at this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, whether you're good enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still slow. I panic a bit when a patient deteriorates and I always call Kofi. He says that's the right thing, but I see the newer ones who seem faster than me already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you cut first if things got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My phone contract, I'd go to a cheap one. And the takeaways after nights. I'd keep the car because buses don't run at seven in the morning when I finish.

say: New tech in the NHS usually ends up as **a new password**.
I'd just shrug in the break room and say **told you**.
think: I'm glad there's **less pressure** to learn things I'm bad at.
With only **two months saved**, rent rises worry me more than AI.
do: Keep working **nights** for the extra pay.
Do the **swallow assessment** training my manager wants.
feel: **Uneasy** about money and about being good enough.
S0.quote: Night shifts on a stroke ward with rent going up every year is already the hard part, with or without AI.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **money and confidence**, not technology.
She leans on **Kofi**, the senior night nurse, more than she'd like.
She'd fall back on her **parents** for a deposit.

steps.text: Keep working nights on the stroke ward for the extra pay
Set aside about £50 a month from each pay packet
Ask her parents to help with the next rental deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and writing. That's the bit I'm worst at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably fine for nurses, because you can't write a care plan for a stroke patient without seeing them. I'd say it's the office people who should worry. I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me a bit. If the care plans and handovers move to some AI system, I'll be the one who can't use it. I still write my handover on paper first and then type it in, because the screen makes me freeze. I don't think I'd lose my job, there's always a shortage, but I'd feel stupid every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see how the others get on with it first, honestly. Then, when I had to, I'd ask Kofi to show me on a quiet night. I'd keep saving and keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the first week after qualifying, when everything felt like a test I was failing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever take a course on it before you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I know I should. I'd tell myself I'm too tired after nights, which is true, but it's also an excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The discharge coordinator, Brenda. She books all the transport and the care packages. That's the whole job on your card.

say: Nurses are probably fine, because you can't plan care **without seeing patients**.
It's the **office people** who should worry, not us.
think: I'd be the one who **can't use** the new AI charting.
I'd keep my job but **feel stupid** every shift.
do: **Wait and see** how others manage with the new system first.
Ask **Kofi** to show me on a quiet night shift.
Keep **saving** and keep my head down.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the first week after qualifying.
S1.quote: I still write my handover on paper first and then type it in, because the screen makes me freeze.
fieldNote: She expects to keep her job but **lose confidence**.
She admits tiredness is partly **an excuse** to avoid learning.
Her public line shifts the risk to **office workers**.

steps.text: Watch how the day team copes with AI charting first
Ask Kofi to show her the new system on a quiet night
Keep putting about £50 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, and then robots three years later. That's not long at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government and the hospitals need to slow it down, test it properly, and make sure there's still a person by the bed. I'd say it to friends, not online. I'm not political, but that seems like common sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I think the computer part goes first and I wouldn't miss it. But by 2031, when the robots can do the lifting, a slow junior nurse who never touches AI is the first name on the list. That's me. I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save as hard as I could, cut the takeaways and the phone, maybe get to four months. I'd go back to my parents' house if I had to, they've got the spare room. I'd think about care home work, because I can't imagine robots in my nan's care home any time soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake after nights, which is hard enough to do anyway. I can't see what I'd retrain into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move back to your parents'. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Embarrassing at twenty-nine. But my mum would love it. My dad would make jokes about robots every dinner, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI now. Would you start, if it bought you time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to. I'd do the minimum, though. I'm not going to become a tech person at this stage.

say: Hospitals should **slow it down** and test it properly.
There should always be **a person** by the bed.
think: I wouldn't miss the **computer part** of the job.
By **2031**, a slow junior who avoids AI goes first.
do: Cut takeaways and phone costs to reach **four months** saved.
Move back to **my parents'** spare room if needed.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake with no idea what to retrain into.
S2.quote: When the robots can do the lifting, a slow junior nurse who never touches AI is the first name on the list.
fieldNote: She clearly expects to be **first to go** once robots arrive.
She'd do only **the minimum** with AI, even to buy time.
Care homes feel **safer** to her, through her nan.

steps.text: Cancel takeaways and switch to a cheaper phone contract
Build savings to four months of costs
Move back into her parents' spare room if money runs short
Apply for nursing jobs in local care homes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. A bit better, but still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing: slow down, test it, keep people at the bedside. Maybe with less panic in my voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years gives me time to get good at the job, but I'd still be racing a robot to 2034. I'd have seven years in by then, which counts for something. But I'd still be a nurse who avoids new tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get really solid at the hands-on stuff: the swallow assessments, the moving and handling. Save steadily. Maybe do a short course on the AI charting when the hospital makes it compulsory, not before. And watch what happens to nurses in other hospitals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not the sleepless kind. More of a background worry I'd carry around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you more willing to learn the tech?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Kofi did it first and said it was fine. I trust him. I don't trust the managers who send emails about 'exciting new systems'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who asked if they should become a nurse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes, still. But I'd say get the degree, not the diploma, and learn the computer stuff early. Don't be like me.

say: Slow down, **test it**, and keep people at the bedside.
I'd say it with **less panic** than the two-year picture.
think: Seven years' experience by **2031** counts for something.
I'd still be a nurse who **avoids new tech**, which worries me.
do: Get **solid** at swallow assessments and moving and handling.
Take the **AI charting course** only when it's compulsory.
**Watch** what happens to nurses in other hospitals.
feel: **Anxious**, as a background worry rather than sleepless nights.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time to get good at the job, but I'd still be racing a robot to 2034.
fieldNote: Extra time helps, but her **reluctance** remains the weak spot.
She trusts **Kofi** far more than managers.
She'd tell others to **get the degree**, admitting her own regret.

steps.text: Get signed off on swallow assessments on the stroke ward
Wait until AI charting training is compulsory before taking it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time in nursing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the hospitals to do it properly, so they've got no excuse. I'd say it in the staff room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, i'd be thirty-seven when the robots come, which is old enough to be scared and young enough to start again. The thinking part goes in 2036 and the hands-on part around 2039. I'd have to decide something by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably do the degree top-up over a few years, if the hospital pays. Not straight away, maybe from 2028. I'd keep saving, keep doing nights, and wait to see what the robots can really do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quietly. Ten years is long, but it still has an end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your nan came up earlier. Why does she matter here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's in a care home on Fern Road and she's lonely. My nan in the care home doesn't need a cleverer computer, she needs someone who knows she takes her tea with two sugars. That's what I'd want people to remember.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the hospital didn't pay for the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I probably wouldn't do it. I'd stay on nights, save, and look at care homes when the time comes.

say: Ten years leaves the hospitals **no excuse** to rush it.
I'd say that in the **staff room**, not online.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** when robots come, scared but young enough to restart.
do: Start a **degree top-up** from about 2028 if the hospital pays.
**Wait** to see what robots can really do.
feel: **Anxious** quietly, because ten years still has an end.
S4.quote: I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come, which is old enough to be scared and young enough to start again.
fieldNote: Even with ten years she stays **anxious**, given low confidence and resistance.
Her plans depend on the **hospital paying**.
Her nan makes the **human side** of care vivid for her.

steps.text: Start a nursing degree top-up from 2028 if the trust pays
Keep working nights on the stroke rehabilitation ward
Wait to see what ward robots can really do before choosing

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, definitely. Two years to the computers and three to the robots, and I'm the slowest nurse on the ward. What would help is the hospital training people like me properly, on paid time, with someone patient, not an e-learning module at four in the morning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the patients and their families. My nan in the care home doesn't need a cleverer computer, she needs someone who knows she takes her tea with two sugars.

headlineQuote: My nan in the care home doesn't need a cleverer computer, she needs someone who knows she takes her tea with two sugars.
portrait: Lena is a **27-year-old junior nurse** working nights on a stroke rehabilitation ward.
She lives alone in a rented flat with only **two months saved** and rising rent.
She **avoids technology** and relies on Kofi, the senior night nurse, to fix her charting.
She's **alarmed** in the fastest picture, expecting to be first to go once robots arrive.
Her fallback ideas are **care home work** and her parents' spare room.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she's the slowest nurse and robots follow within three years.
whatWouldHelp: Hospitals **training staff** properly on paid time with someone patient.
Keeping a **human focus** on patients and families like her nan.
